hints: Think about the word closed first. In Fig. 4.1, does blood ever leave the tubes it travels in, or does it stay inside vessels all the way round?
Now think about the word double. Follow one red blood cell round Fig. 4.1 - how many times does it go through the heart before it gets back to where it started, and which two circuits does it use?
walkthrough:
Closed Means Blood Stays Inside Vessels**
Blood is always enclosed in the heart and blood vessels - arteries, capillaries and veins. It never flows freely in body cavities. Tissue fluid leaks out at capillaries, but red blood cells and most plasma stay inside, so this is different from an open system in insects.

Double Means Two Circuits Through The Heart Twice**
Trace the loop in Fig. 4.1. One circuit goes heart to lungs and back - the pulmonary circulation for gas exchange. The second goes heart to the rest of the body, head, kidneys, liver, intestines, limbs and back - the systemic circulation. Blood goes through the heart twice per full turn, which keeps pressure high for fast delivery.

Final answer: Closed: blood is contained within blood vessels (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries) and does not bathe tissues directly. Double: blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit, in pulmonary circulation (heart to lungs and back) and systemic circulation (heart to rest of body and back).

hints: Start with blood flow direction. Find the thick vessel leaving the left side of the heart to supply the whole body - which large artery must W be?
Now look at X bringing blood back from the lungs to the left side of the heart. Is blood in lung veins oxygenated or deoxygenated, and what are lung veins called?
Y is a valve inside the heart on the right side between atrium and ventricle. Recall the names for right versus left atrioventricular valves.
Z is the upper chamber on the left that receives blood from X. Which atrium collects oxygenated blood from the lungs?
walkthrough:
Follow Oxygenated Blood Out And Back**
W leaves the left ventricle and arches over to supply the head, upper limbs and lower body, so it is the aorta. X carries blood from the lungs back to the left side of the heart with the arrow pointing down toward the heart, so it is the pulmonary vein. Remember pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood, unlike most veins.

Identify The Right Valve And Left Receiving Chamber**
Y sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, so it is the right atrioventricular valve, also called the tricuspid valve because it has three cusps. Z is the left upper chamber receiving X from the lungs, so it is the left atrium. It then passes blood to the left ventricle to be pumped into W.
Final answer: W = aorta / aortic arch; X = pulmonary vein; Y = right atrioventricular / tricuspid valve; Z = left atrium / auricle.

hints: Compare P in a blood vessel with Q in a lymph vessel. Lymph forms from tissue fluid squeezed out of blood capillaries - which large cells or large proteins are too big to leave the blood?
walkthrough:
What Cannot Leave The Capillary**
At P you have whole blood. Fluid, small solutes and white blood cells can leave capillaries to form tissue fluid and then lymph at Q. Red blood cells are too large to pass through the capillary wall pores, so they stay in blood and are absent from lymph. Platelets and large plasma proteins are also retained in blood.
Final answer: Red blood cells (accept platelets or plasma proteins).

hints: Picture air in the alveolus next to deoxygenated blood arriving at the lung. Which gas is high in each place, so which way will each gas move?
Recall the mechanism for this short-distance movement of gases - no pumps or carriers are needed.
Think about the barrier itself. How many cell layers must gases cross, and what type of thin cells make the distance very short?
For continuous fast exchange the gradients must not disappear. What brings fresh air and removes oxygenated blood to keep the difference steep?
walkthrough:
Gases Move By Diffusion Down Gradients**
Alveolar air is high in oxygen and low in carbon dioxide. Incoming pulmonary blood is low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide. So oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out into the alveolus, both from high to low concentration.

Cross A Very Thin Two-Cell Barrier**
Gases cross the squamous epithelium of the alveolus wall and the squamous endothelium of the capillary wall. Together with fused basement membranes this gives a diffusion distance of less than a micrometre, and oxygen then enters red blood cells where it binds haemoglobin.

Gradients Are Kept Steep**
Ventilation brings in fresh oxygen-rich air and removes carbon dioxide-rich air. Continuous blood flow brings deoxygenated blood and carries oxygenated blood away, and haemoglobin loading keeps free oxygen low in blood. This maintains steep diffusion gradients for rapid exchange.

Final answer: Oxygen diffuses from alveolus into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveolus, down concentration gradients; across squamous epithelium of alveolar wall and endothelium of capillary wall into red blood cells; steep gradient maintained by ventilation and by blood flow / uptake by haemoglobin carrying oxygen away.

hints: Look at F pointing to the dark spot inside the large pale nucleus in the TEM. What dense structure inside the nucleus makes ribosomes?
Look at G pointing to the outer edge of the lower cell facing the gut lumen. What boundary separates the cell cytoplasm from the outside?
walkthrough:
Read The TEM Labels**
F points to the small very electron-dense dot inside the nucleus, which is the nucleolus where ribosomal RNA is made. G points to the outer limiting boundary of the epithelial cell on the lumen side, which is the cell surface membrane, also called the plasma membrane.
Final answer: F = nucleolus (accept nucleus); G = cell surface / plasma membrane.

hints: Glucose is too large and polar to pass directly through the lipid bilayer at S, so what kind of membrane protein must help it?
Think about why only glucose and similar sugars use this route and not other molecules - what does that tell you about the protein?
Compare this to active transport. Does glucose need ATP here, and which way down or up its concentration gradient does it move out toward the capillary?
walkthrough:
Needs A Specific Carrier Protein**
At the basal surface S, glucose leaves through a transporter or carrier protein spanning the membrane. The protein has a specific binding site that fits glucose, so only glucose or very similar molecules can bind. That specificity is the hallmark of facilitated diffusion.

Binding Causes Shape Change, No Energy Needed**
When glucose binds, the protein changes shape - a conformational change - and opens to the other side to release glucose toward the capillary. This is passive: movement is down the concentration gradient from high glucose in the epithelial cell to lower glucose in tissue fluid and blood, so no ATP is used.

Final answer: Via specific transporter / carrier protein with glucose binding site; glucose binding causes conformational / shape change to release glucose on other side; passive process requiring no ATP / no energy, movement down concentration gradient from high to low concentration.
